mechanisms.mechanism: Pure death-attrition, no emigration, no refusal gate. Starvation if food supply falls below ~100 food/person/year; freezing if firewood/coal stock runs out or a colonist is caught outdoors in winter without tailor-made warm clothing. No 'leave the map' mechanic exists at all -- net population is births minus these two death causes, read via rising/falling child count.
mechanisms.applicability: Directly analogous to Bastion's hunger system except Bastion's hunger currently CANNOT kill (downed=0 across 4,867 samples). Adopting this model means reopening that invariant, not just adding a Contract arm.

mechanisms.mechanism: Per-pawn, mood-gated, stochastic and reversible. Mental Break Threshold defaults to 35% mood; Major break triggers at 4/7 of that (~20%), Extreme at 1/7 (~5%). Below threshold each pawn rolls a periodic chance of a break; severe breaks include the pawn wandering off and being permanently lost. Separately, sustained starvation stacks a malnutrition condition that can kill on its own, independent of mood.
mechanisms.applicability: Closest fit to an individual-level, need-driven loss mechanic. Would require Bastion to define an analogous per-colonist mood-collapse state and a real probability curve, rather than a scripted departure -- more machinery than the ColonyDrive tree currently has.

mechanisms.mechanism: Unhappy dwarves tantrum (destroy property, fight, cancel jobs) rather than leave; if a tantrum kills someone, the grief of surviving family triggers further tantrums -- a self-reinforcing 'tantrum spiral' that can destroy the fort. Population loss is entirely a byproduct of the violence/starvation/thirst the spiral causes, never migration out. No emigration mechanic exists; unhappy dwarves become non-functional or violent in place.
mechanisms.applicability: Shows a design that deliberately has NO exit valve -- unhappiness converts to internal violence/dysfunction, not population loss. Relevant as a cautionary counter-example, not a template, given Bastion already has a Defend arm that could absorb unrest instead.

mechanisms.mechanism: Explicit, symmetric, rate-bounded approval gate on both migration directions. At 50% approval: +1 family/month moves in if housing is free. At 75%+: up to +2 families/month. At <20% approval: -1 family LEAVES per month. Independently, running out of granary stock over winter causes outright starvation deaths regardless of approval. Fully reversible -- raising approval back above the floor resumes inflow.
mechanisms.applicability: Structurally the closest match to a Contract arm mirroring Bastion's existing Grow arm: same signal (approval/mood) gates both directions, sheds by household (consistent with HOUSING IS BEDS), and gives a concrete rate (households/game-day) to pin against a fixture.

mechanisms.mechanism: Immigration switches on above 80% happiness and scales toward 100%. Emigration on low happiness existed for free citizens in earlier versions but was DELIBERATELY REMOVED by the developer; now only enslaved population can flee (a bondage-specific mechanic), while unhappy free citizens riot/turn violent instead of leaving.
mechanisms.applicability: A load-bearing negative data point: a genre peer tried per-citizen emigration-on-unhappiness and walked it back in favor of an unrest response. Argues against assuming emigration is obviously the right shape for Bastion's Contract arm.

mechanisms.mechanism: No per-citizen emigration or refusal exists. Hope and Discontent are city-wide meters, not population counters: Hope sustained at 0% or Discontent sustained near 100% triggers a binary game-over (people give up / uprising), not gradual population loss. Individual death (illness, cold exposure, accidents) is a separate, disconnected system. The one real population-control lever is upstream: players can explicitly refuse incoming refugee groups.
mechanisms.applicability: Models capacity control entirely upstream (refuse arrivals) rather than downstream (shed existing colonists) -- relevant to Bastion's Grow/Expand gate but does not by itself resolve an ALREADY-over-capacity town like the 46-in-10-houses case.

research.recommendation: Adopt the Manor Lords shape for a Contract arm: gate emigration off the same mood/approval signal that already gates Grow, symmetrically, at a bounded rate (their reference number: -1 household/month once approval sits under a floor, reversing automatically once it recovers). It reuses Bastion's existing house/bed accounting (sheds by household per the HOUSING IS BEDS ruling) instead of inventing new death machinery, and it is the only one of the six with a concrete, citable rate rather than a vague 'people leave when unhappy.' Song of Syx's own retraction of per-citizen emigration is the strongest reason NOT to assume this is automatically correct -- flag it to the owner alongside the recommendation.
research.what_would_falsify: Build the over-capacity fixture (roster > sum of house capacity, mood/approval held under the departure floor) and run it N consecutive game-days. If departures don't track the trigger -- a happy-but-overcrowded town still empties out, or a miserable-but-under-capacity town never sheds anyone -- the mechanism is wired to the wrong condition (mood alone vs. capacity-overflow alone vs. the AND of both, which is what Manor Lords' approval-gates-housing-assignment implicitly requires) and needs re-deriving before it ships.
research.question: POPULATION CONTRACTION: Bastion's ColonyDrive has no Contract arm, so an over-capacity town (46 colonists / 10 houses) froze for 86 game days with no mechanism to shed population. What do Banished, RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, Manor Lords, Song of Syx, and Frostpunk do, and is 'should a town shed population' a design judgement call?

What mechanism do colony sims / 4X games use to trade terrain difficulty against resource/settlement capacity when scoring a founding site, and what scoring shape would let Bastion's autofound keep 'flat wins among adequate sites' without 'flat wins over any site regardless of capacity'?

mechanisms.mechanism: The Site Finder exposes ~14 independent sliders (Elevation/Flat, Aquifer, Savagery, Evil, Temperature, Rain, Drainage, Flux Stone, River, Shallow/Deep Metal, Soil, Clay, Biome count). Each is either N/A (contributes zero weight) or set to a target value. The wiki states the algorithm explicitly: a setting other than N/A 'does not guarantee an exact match... the finder will then display the candidate that best fit as many as possible of the selected settings of the desired size.' This is a multi-criteria satisficing match (effectively a count/weighted-sum of satisfied preferences), not a lexicographic sort — no single criterion, flatness included, is a hard first-key gate that can exclude an otherwise-strong site. Separately, the wiki documents a real-world instance of exactly Bastion's mountain-confound bug: elevation statistics are computed per 16x16 REGION, not per embark tile, so 'if a 16x16 region is completely flat, but has one tall mountain in one far corner... you still have all the empty air of the highest mountain in every embark tile' — a coarse-grained stat poisoning locally-flat sites.
mechanisms.applicability: Directly rebuts pure lexicographic-with-binary-first-key scoring: DF's genre-defining site tool treats flatness as one weighted preference among many, never a categorical veto. Also flags a second thing worth auditing in Bastion independent of the scoring formula: whether alt_range is sampled at the site's own local footprint or at some coarser region/chunk granularity that could itself be a mountain-confound vector, separate from how the value gets weighted.

mechanisms.game: Civilization V / VI — AI settler site evaluation
mechanisms.mechanism: CvSiteEvaluationClasses.cpp (PlotFoundValue, in the Firaxis-released modding SDK source) runs a genuine two-stage evaluator. Stage 1 is a small set of true hard-fail categorical exclusions — isImpassable(), isMountain(), isWater() — plots that fail these are simply not legal city sites, full stop. Every plot that survives Stage 1 is then scored by an ADDITIVE weighted sum of independent yield sub-scores: iFoodValue = ComputeFoodValue(...) * GC.getSETTLER_FOOD_MULTIPLIER() (15), iProductionValue = ComputeProductionValue(...) * SETTLER_PRODUCTION_MULTIPLIER (3), plus a gold term (multiplier 2), with percentage BONUSES layered on top rather than gates — river +BUILD_ON_RIVER_PERCENT (15%), coastal +SETTLER_BUILD_ON_COAST_PERCENT (40%) — and ring-distance modifiers ([6, 3, ...]) that taper contribution by proximity to the city center. Hilliness isn't even a separate bucket; it feeds production yield like any other tile attribute.
mechanisms.source: https://github.com/Gedemon/Civ5-DLL/blob/master/CvGameCoreDLL_Expansion2/CvSiteEvaluationClasses.cpp (fetched directly; Firaxis's public Civ5 DLL modding source)
mechanisms.applicability: This is the closest existing pattern to 'minimum-capacity floor before flatness': a hard floor excludes only genuinely-illegal ground (in Bastion's terms: unbuildable, not merely hilly), and everything that clears the floor competes on a weighted additive sum where no single term can lexicographically dominate — a site with much higher yield-sum can always outscore a marginally-better-terrain site, and vice versa when yields are close. The tunable multiplier constants (exposed as engine constants, i.e. designer knobs) are the direct precedent for 'weights are an owner judgment call, but the two-stage SHAPE is not.'

mechanisms.game: RimWorld — world tile / landing site selection
mechanisms.mechanism: Vanilla RimWorld computes no combined numeric score at all. World tile hilliness (Flat / Small Hills / Large Hills / Mountains) is one of several independent, orthogonal attributes (biome, temperature, rainfall, growing period, coastal, roads, stone types) that the game surfaces to the player as separate readouts; the player free-picks any tile or hits 'random.' The community filtering tool PrepareLanding formalizes this as independently-combinable filters rather than a fused rank, with its own docs framing the design goal explicitly: the player, not a formula, is 'the master of your fate.'
mechanisms.source: https://neitsa.github.io/games/rimworld/preparelanding/starting.html ; https://rimworldwiki.com/wiki/World_generation (categorical hilliness confirmed; vanilla scoring formula not documented because none exists)
mechanisms.applicability: A second valid genre answer to the same problem: don't fuse terrain and capacity into one order at all. If Bastion's autofound is meant to assist rather than dictate, presenting separate top-N lists ('flattest adequate site' vs 'highest-capacity site') sidesteps the domination problem entirely instead of trying to get one weighting formula right — a fallback worth naming even though it doesn't answer 'what single mechanism,' since it's what RimWorld chose on purpose.

mechanisms.game: Banished / Manor Lords — map & settlement placement
mechanisms.mechanism: No comparable per-tile capacity-vs-flatness scoring mechanism was found for either game. Banished has no autofound at all — the player free-places every building on hand-inspected terrain, so there is no algorithm to borrow. Manor Lords offers the player a handful of pre-authored starting regions from a menu (procedurally generated at a coarse, whole-region grain) rather than scoring individual founding tiles continuously; guides describe players manually eyeballing 'the largest flat corridor' rather than the game ranking sites for them.
mechanisms.source: https://gamerant.com/manor-lords-where-build-your-first-settlement/ ; https://www.dexerto.com/gaming/best-layout-for-settlement-development-in-manor-lords-2674305/ (secondary, gameplay-guide level only — no generation-algorithm documentation surfaced)
mechanisms.applicability: Not applicable as prior art for a scoring formula — flagged as an absence rather than forced into a false citation, per the project's own evidence-craft rules against reading a grep hit as more than it is.

research.recommendation: Adopt Civilization 5/6's two-stage shape (floor, then weighted sum), calibrated by Dwarf Fortress's principle that flatness must be one weighted term among several rather than a sole gate: Stage 1 is a hard, capacity-based floor — a site must clear a minimum houses/fields (or combined buildable-capacity) threshold to be a candidate at all, replacing the current situation where a 2-house/1-field site is even eligible to beat a 10-house/2-field site. Stage 2 scores every site that clears the floor with an additive weighted sum — score = w_flat*flatness_term + w_fields*fields + w_houses*houses − w_dist*distance — where flatness_term is graded (continuous, e.g. proportional to (K − alt_range) clamped at 0, or at minimum a 3+ tier bucket) instead of today's binary alt_range<=8 cutoff. This preserves 'flat wins among sites that are otherwise close' (as DF's multi-criteria match and Civ5's yield-sum both do) while making it possible for a large enough capacity gap to outweigh a modest flatness gap — which no lexicographic sort with a binary first key can ever express, regardless of how the later keys are ordered. Also borrow DF's documented mountain-confound precedent as a second check: verify alt_range is sampled at the candidate site's own local footprint, not a coarser region/chunk grain, independent of the weighting fix.
research.what_would_falsify: Re-run the 42-site / 16,384-block search under floor+weighted-sum scoring with a range of non-degenerate weights (w_flat > 0 but not dominant). If the owner's 10-house/2-field/alt_range-80.8 town still cannot beat the 2-house/1-field flat site under ANY choice of weights that leaves flatness meaningfully influential (i.e., you'd have to set w_flat to effectively zero to make the 10-house site win), then the scoring SHAPE isn't the actual defect — the real bug is upstream of scoring (candidate generation truncating the search, alt_range being sampled at the wrong granularity the way DF's region-level stat is, or the search radius culling the 10-house site's candidate cell before it's ever scored), and that must be found and fixed instead of, or in addition to, changing the formula.

research.question: When and how much farmland should bastion add autonomously, and by what rule/unit?

mechanisms.mechanism: Farm plots are 100% player-designated tiles; there is no in-game AI that adds them. The wiki's converged community heuristic is a per-capita TILE ratio derived by back-solving yield vs. consumption: each dwarf eats/drinks 7 units/season (196/yr); a 3x3 plot (9 tiles) of plump helmets yields enough alcohol+food for ~95 dwarves (~0.095 tiles/dwarf), a 5x5 (25 tiles) supports ~265 dwarves (~0.094 tiles/dwarf), and 50 tiles is the quoted 'never need more' ceiling (~0.2 tiles/dwarf conservative incl. variety/cloth crops). The ratio itself is (population x per-capita consumption/season) / (plot yield per tile per season).
mechanisms.applicability: No autonomous-placement precedent to borrow (player draws every plot). What transfers is the UNIT: a fixed per-capita tile ratio computed from measured yield-per-tile and measured consumption-per-dwarf, exactly the same shape as bastion's MATURE/day (yield) vs EatFrom/day (consumption).

mechanisms.mechanism: Fields are placed entirely by the player; no auto-expansion. Community-derived ratio: ~100 food/person/year consumption; a well-placed farmer covers 80-90 tiles yielding ~7 food/tile (~600 food/farmer at full efficiency); guidance is roughly 30-40% of the workforce on food once population is educated/diversified. No stock-below-par trigger exists in-engine -- barns just display current stock, and running out is a player-visible failure state, not a triggered response.
mechanisms.applicability: Same shape as DF: a per-worker/per-tile production-vs-consumption ratio the player must maintain manually. No automatic trigger mechanism exists to copy; only the ratio-math is reusable.

mechanisms.mechanism: Growing zones are manually drawn rectangles (drag-and-place); vanilla has no auto-expansion. Consumption is precisely defined: ~1.6 nutrition/colonist/day (~2 meals/day). Community calculators back-solve plants-needed-per-colonist from crop yield/growth-days vs that 1.6/day figure (e.g. ~21-30 plants/colonist depending on crop and soil). This is a pure projected-consumption model: (colonists x nutrition/day) / (plant yield / days-to-maturity) = plants (hence zone tiles) required.
mechanisms.applicability: Closest structural match to bastion's own numbers: nutrition/day is bastion's hunger-decay constant (0.000889/sec ~ 1 meal/colonist/game-day), and plant yield/growth-days is bastion's MATURE-per-field-per-day. RimWorld's community formula is essentially the same equation bastion would need, just player-executed instead of engine-executed.

mechanisms.mechanism: Farm/orchard/pasture zones are player-designated (moisture- and soil-gated); no auto-placement. The game's economy panel surfaces a live stock-trend gauge -- net days-of-food-stored, i.e. production-minus-consumption projected forward -- which is the closest of the six to an explicit 'trend toward par' readout a system could act on. Community reports show the ratio breaking down around pop ~250 (food production can't scale without dedicating ~50% of workforce to it), i.e. players hit a wall the live gauge warned them about but the game itself never auto-corrects.
mechanisms.applicability: Contributes the STOCK-TREND framing (days-of-food-remaining, not just a static stock<par flag) -- bastion could compute an analogous 'days until food_stock hits par at current MATURE/day minus EatFrom/day' projection rather than a bare threshold, catching a slide before stock actually crosses par.

mechanisms.mechanism: Burgage-plot fields are entirely player-laid; consumption is a hard per-family (roughly 1 food-type/family/month, with variety tiers gating happiness) and granary logistics is a real ratio: 1 stall serves ~40 families, 1 granary-worker family per ~50-60 villagers, a fully-staffed farmhouse manages 4 fields per crop cycle (so ~2 farmhouses per 12 fields incl. fallow rotation). Again no auto-trigger -- granary UI just shows current stock and a food-variety/consumption breakdown per plot.
mechanisms.applicability: Contributes a WORKER-CAPACITY constraint bastion doesn't yet model: even with land available, a fixed number of farmhands can only tend N fields per cycle. If bastion ever auto-places fields, it should also check colonist labor capacity, not just stone/tiles, mirroring the housing gate's stone>=20 resource check.

mechanisms.mechanism: Farm buildings are player-placed but sized against a fixed per-population-tier consumption table baked into the game (e.g. one potato farm's throughput is calibrated to supply up to 600 Farmer-tier residents, fewer as residences upgrade to higher tiers with different diets). The needs UI shows a live percentage surplus/deficit per consumer good per island, which is the most directly 'par-vs-actual' style live gauge among all six games, but placement of new farms in response is still 100% manual.
mechanisms.applicability: Contributes the SURPLUS/DEFICIT-PERCENTAGE framing (production capacity / demand, expressed as a ratio around 100%, with color-coded warning before the good actually runs out) -- functionally identical to computing bastion's (fields x MATURE/day) / (roster x EatFrom/day) as a live percentage and gating new fields on that percentage falling under a threshold, rather than waiting for food_stock to cross par.

research.recommendation: No prior-art game actually auto-places farmland -- in all six, plot/zone/field placement is 100% manual; the AI-driven trigger bastion wants (parallel to its house gate) has no literal precedent to copy verbatim. What IS consistent across all six is the UNIT and the MATH: every game (or its community) reduces the question to a projected-consumption ratio -- (population x per-capita consumption rate) vs (plot count x yield rate per growth cycle) -- expressed as either a per-capita tile count (DF, Banished, RimWorld) or a live surplus/deficit percentage (Anno, Song of Syx). Recommend building bastion's farm-expansion gate on exactly that ratio using inputs it already logs: per_capita_demand = hunger-decay-derived ~1 meal/colonist/game-day (bastion's own EatFrom/day observation validates this); per_field_supply = MATURE per field per day; coverage_ratio = (fields x per_field_supply) / (roster x per_capita_demand). Gate a new field the way the house gate works (houses < roster+1 && stone>=20 -> place bed): add a field when coverage_ratio drops under a threshold (e.g. <1.5, giving buffer for the multi-day grow cycle, mirroring RimWorld/DF community margins of ~1.3-2x raw need) AND that drop persists across a full game-day window (per the 'burst sample reads as structural gap' law already in bastion's memory) rather than reacting to a single tick of food_stock<par, since food_stock alone lags the true signal by an entire crop-maturation cycle. This is a projected-consumption model expressed in bastion's native units, not a raw stock-below-par reactive trigger and not a fixed field-count-per-roster constant.
research.what_would_falsify: Compute coverage_ratio = (fields x MATURE/day) / (roster x ~1 meal/colonist/day) at the actual maximum roster bastion's growth loop self-limits to (per the handoff notes, population growth already caps itself once Expand ends -- check the current observed ceiling). If that ratio stays comfortably >1 (e.g. matches or exceeds the already-measured 13x margin) all the way to that ceiling, the recommended mechanism is falsified as unnecessary: bastion's single field is already over-provisioned relative to every reference game's per-capita heuristic, and no autonomous farm-expansion gate is needed before some other cap (housing, stone, colonist labor per Manor Lords' farmhouse-capacity precedent) binds first. Conversely, if a 3-replicate measurement (per the colony-metrics-need-three-replicates law) shows coverage_ratio crossing below ~1.5 at any roster size bastion actually reaches, that measurement is what justifies building the gate now rather than deferring it.

research.question: Bastion caches a per-colonist trunk route (path_cache: waypoints + index) and invalidates it only on >3-cell target drift, never on terrain change. The colony now builds (places blocks), so a cached route can pass through a wall that didn't exist when planned. A ~5-per-10k 'waypoint inside rock' embed residual was hypothesized to be this; the builds_since_route instrument is in but under-sampled. What mechanism do Minecraft mods, Dwarf Fortress, RimWorld, and general game AI use to invalidate cached paths on world edit — dirty regions, chunk version counters, per-step revalidation on advance, or full re-plan — and which fits a per-colonist waypoint+index cache with a cheap per-tick advance loop?

mechanisms.game: MineColonies (built on ldtteam/PerViamInvenire, the actual pathfinding library MineColonies ships)
mechanisms.mechanism: There is NO terrain-change listener. PerViamInvenireGroundPathNavigator.recomputePath() is a literal empty override -- placing a block never pings any in-flight path. Invalidation is entirely progress-based: every tick, CallbackBasedStuckHandler.checkStuck() compares path.getNextNodeIndex() to last tick's index and checks whether the entity moved >1.5 blocks in the last 100 ticks (lastStuckCheck). If not, it calls navigator.stopCurrentCalculation() to force a fresh path job. In parallel, doStuckDetection() computes an expected-travel-time-per-node from distance/mob-speed and drops the path if wall-clock time exceeds 3x that estimate. Unstuck then escalates by level: L0 clear+replan (600-tick cooldown), L1 replan+moveAway (300-tick cooldown), L2 skip-ahead teleport along the existing path, and a global-timeout 'complete stuck' action that can teleport the mob to goal and/or break blocks in front of it.
mechanisms.source: https://github.com/ldtteam/PerViamInvenire -- src/main/java/com/ldtteam/perviaminvenire/pathfinding/PerViamInvenireGroundPathNavigator.java (recomputePath, doStuckDetection, lines ~731-774) and src/api/java/com/ldtteam/perviaminvenire/api/pathfinding/stuckhandling/CallbackBasedStuckHandler.java (checkStuck/tryUnstuck/completeStuckAction, lines ~134-310), branch version/latest, fetched directly via raw.githubusercontent.com and the GitHub trees API
mechanisms.applicability: Same structural blind spot Bastion has: no write-side hook on block placement. The part that DOES transfer for free onto a waypoints+index cache is the O(1) per-tick 'did the index advance, are we roughly where expected' check -- it costs nothing extra since the advance loop already reads the entity's position every tick. But relying on stuck-detection ALONE means a colonist walks up to and stalls at the new wall for up to ~100 ticks (or 3x the per-node travel estimate) before anything fires -- that stall-then-recover window is a worse symptom than Bastion's embed, not a better one. It converts an instant walk-through-wall into a longer visible stall, it does not prevent the bad frame.

mechanisms.mechanism: Every walkable cell carries a region/zone index from an optimized flood-fill, so a colonist rejects an unreachable destination in O(1) without ever running A*. On any edifice edit (wall placed/removed, door added) the affected cells are pushed into a RegionDirtyer -- this is cheap and IMMEDIATE, just setting dirty bits (SetAllDirty / per-cell dirty). The expensive part is deferred and batched: RegionAndRoomUpdater.TryRebuildDirtyRegionsAndRooms() runs once per pass (effectively once per tick), is guarded by a re-entrancy flag ('working'), checks regionDirtyer.AnyDirty, and if set regenerates regions from ONLY the dirty cells, rebuilds rooms, recombines region/room groups, then SetAllClean(). Pattern: mark-dirty-immediately-at-the-edit-site, rebuild-lazily-in-one-batched-pass, touching only what changed.
mechanisms.source: Tynan Sylvester, "Reachability at last," Ludeon Studios dev blog, 5 Jul 2013, https://ludeon.com/blog/2013/07/reachability-at-last/ (states the design intent directly: 'I'll need to detect changed conditions like walls being built or blown up and regenerate the local reachability indexes'); mechanism confirmed against decompiled shipped source: https://github.com/josh-m/RW-Decompile/blob/master/Verse/RegionAndRoomUpdater.cs (TryRebuildDirtyRegionsAndRooms, RegenerateNewRegionsFromDirtyCells, regionDirtyer.AnyDirty/SetAllDirty/SetAllClean)
mechanisms.applicability: This is the closest matched pattern to what Bastion is actually missing: a write-side hook at the point of block placement, cheap because the mark is O(1) and the rebuild is deferred+batched rather than synchronous. It doesn't map onto Bastion's cache structure directly (Bastion has no region graph), but the pattern generalizes cleanly: on block-place, mark the block's chunk/column dirty; any colonist whose cached waypoint list has a waypoint in a dirty chunk gets its cache index invalidated the next time it's ticked -- cheap immediate mark, deferred clear, scoped to the colonists actually affected instead of a global rescan.

mechanisms.mechanism: DF computes connected-component 'walkability groups' via flood-fill and tries to patch them incrementally (flood outward from the changed area) rather than recomputing globally, so in principle a dig or wall-build should only touch the local region of the flood-fill. In practice this incremental cache is documented to desync specifically around construction events -- wall/floor building, wall teardown, digging -- leaving individual dwarves believing a 1-4 tile pocket is cut off from the rest of the fortress when it physically is not. The only confirmed fixes in the bug report are forcing a hard invalidation through an unrelated state toggle (locking then unlocking a door) or a full save/reload -- both force a clean, non-incremental recompute rather than trusting the local patch.
mechanisms.source: Dwarf Fortress Bug Tracker #12665, "Pathfinding breaks locally for single dwarves after path changes (wall building, floor building, wall tear down, digging)," https://dwarffortressbugtracker.com/view.php?id=12665 (primary, dated, reproducible bug report with confirmed workarounds). The underlying flood-fill/walkability-group description is community-sourced from search results, not a single canonical Bay12 dev post -- treat that part as from memory/community-summarized, unverified against primary Toady One commentary.
mechanisms.applicability: This is the cautionary case the question flags DF for, and it is directly on-point: an incremental, edit-local invalidation cache is easy to get subtly wrong exactly at the edit boundary, producing the same class of symptom Bastion has (a mismatch between where a route thinks it can go and what the terrain now is) but in the opposite direction -- a false 'blocked' rather than a false 'open'. Lesson for Bastion: if the fix scopes invalidation to 'only colonists/paths near this edit,' the neighborhood test at the boundary must be conservative (over-invalidate at the margin) or Bastion trades a rare embed-in-rock bug for a rare stuck-forever-thinking-it's-blocked bug of the same DF shape.

mechanisms.game: General game AI -- D* Lite / Anytime Dynamic A* (incremental replanning search)
mechanisms.mechanism: Maintains a g-value and rhs-value (one-step lookahead) per node from the previous solve. A changed edge cost (a cell flipping passable->blocked) marks only the node(s) touching that edge as 'locally inconsistent' and reinserts them into a priority queue; the algorithm re-expands ONLY inconsistent nodes, propagating the repair outward until consistency is restored, instead of rerunning A* from scratch. Repair cost scales with the number of changed edges and how far the inconsistency propagates, not with map size. Documented practical caveat: when the change is structurally large (not one cell) or propagation exceeds a time/expansion budget, systems built on D* Lite commonly ABORT the incremental repair and fall back to a from-scratch replan, because in that regime incremental repair can cost more than a fresh solve.
mechanisms.source: S. Koenig & M. Likhachev, "D* Lite," AAAI 2002 (from memory, unverified against the original PDF this session); overview corroborated via https://dibyendu-biswas.medium.com/d-d-lite-lpa-e7483779a7ca and the survey https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03735 ("On dynamic multi-agent pathfinding methods"); the abort-to-full-replan-on-large-change caveat also corroborated there; Likhachev et al., "Anytime Dynamic A*," http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ggordon/likhachev-etal.anytime-dstar.pdf
mechanisms.applicability: Architecturally too heavy to retrofit directly: D* Lite needs a persistent search graph (g/rhs per node) kept alive per agent between ticks, a different data shape than Bastion's flat 'waypoints + index' and real bookkeeping cost multiplied across colony population. The transferable IDEA rather than the machinery: a changed cell should invalidate only the (small) set of live routes whose EXISTING waypoints touch that exact cell/column, not a global re-plan and not nothing. And the 'abort incremental repair for a from-scratch replan past a change-size threshold' rule is functionally the same shape as Bastion's existing >3-cell target-drift full-replan trigger -- Bastion already has this fallback wired to target movement; the recommendation is to wire the same fallback to terrain edits near the route, not to invent a new mechanism.

mechanisms.game: Navmesh dynamic-obstacle rebuilds (Recast/Detour TileCache; the general pattern behind Unity/Unreal runtime navmesh updates)
mechanisms.mechanism: Dynamic-world navmeshes are tiled (a fixed-size grid of tiles over the world). An added/removed/moved obstacle is mapped to the tile(s) whose bounding box it touches (inflated by a border for correct edge-stitching); ONLY those tiles are re-voxelized/rebuilt and swapped back into the mesh -- everything else is untouched. Detour's TileCache variant is cheaper still for simple obstacle shapes (cylinders/boxes): it keeps a compressed per-tile heightfield and applies/removes obstacle markers without a full Recast rebuild, so a single obstacle add/remove is an incremental op, not a tile rebuild. An agent's path is checked against the CURRENT navmesh as its corridor is followed/advanced each step -- there is no active push notification to agents; staleness is caught passively at advance time.
mechanisms.source: Mikko Mononen (Recast's author), "Handling Temporary Obstacles," Digesting Duck blog, Aug 2010, http://digestingduck.blogspot.com/2010/08/handling-temporary-obstacles.html ; recastnavigation project discussion threads on dynamic tiles and obstacles: https://groups.google.com/g/recastnavigation/c/B70jSpTzVsI and https://groups.google.com/g/recastnavigation/c/CJNtbRIb_Xc
mechanisms.applicability: Direct industry analogue of 'chunk-scoped dirty rebuild' -- tile maps almost exactly onto Bastion's chunk/column concept. The 'check the path against current world state passively as you advance' half of this pattern is the single cheapest, most directly applicable piece: since Bastion's advance loop already reads the next waypoint's cell to move the colonist into it, that same read can also ask 'is this cell still passable' at zero extra world-query cost, and only fall back to a fresh plan if it isn't.

mechanisms.mechanism: No specific cache-invalidation mechanism was found in public sources. Marketing/changelog copy for the mod mentions general 'smoother navigation around walls, stairs and paths' and fixes for 'pathfinding teleport glitches' across versions, but nothing describing an actual invalidation algorithm, cache structure, or trigger condition.
mechanisms.source: From memory / unverified -- searched https://www.millenaire.org/ and CurseForge/9Minecraft listings, found no technical writeup or source-level detail; the mod's source is on GitHub but was not inspected this session.
mechanisms.applicability: Not usable as prior art here beyond the general observation that a well-known village-builder mod in the same genre as Bastion has publicly reported the identical class of symptom ('pathfinding teleport glitches,' 'builders getting stuck') that terrain-unaware path caches produce -- weak circumstantial support that this is a common, recurring failure mode in this exact genre, not evidence of a specific mechanism to copy.

research.recommendation: Do not copy any single game wholesale (full D* Lite graph repair is too heavy for a per-colonist flat cache; a full RimWorld-style region graph is too big a rewrite; MineColonies' stuck-detection-only approach just converts the embed into a longer visible stall). Instead, combine the two cheapest pieces that showed up independently across every source and that both bolt onto the EXISTING path_cache (waypoints + index) without restructuring it: (1) per-step revalidation on advance -- at the top of the per-tick advance loop, before moving the colonist into path_cache.waypoints[index], check whether that cell is still passable. This is the Recast/Detour TileCache pattern ('check the path against current world state passively as you advance') and it costs nothing extra: the advance loop already reads that cell to move the colonist into it. On failure, trigger a full re-plan from the colonist's current position -- reusing the SAME full-replan path Bastion's existing >3-cell-drift trigger already uses, which is also the same 'abort to full replan on a large/structural change' fallback D* Lite implementations use. (2) event-scoped invalidation at build time -- on block placement, walk the (small) set of colonists whose remaining waypoints fall in the placed block's chunk/column and clear just those caches. This is RimWorld's dirty-mark-now/rebuild-lazily pattern, scoped by chunk instead of a full region graph, and it is what actually prevents the embed frame rather than recovering from it a tick later like (1) alone would. Neither piece requires storing a region graph, a version counter per chunk, or a persistent search graph per agent -- both are O(1) amortized against the work Bastion's per-tick loop and build-placement code already do.
research.what_would_falsify: Instrument the per-step check in (1) to log every time it fires (next-waypoint-cell found solid) and cross-reference against builds_since_route from the existing instrument, across at least 3 replicate runs per the project's own colony-metrics-variance rule. Falsified if: (a) the ~5-per-10k 'waypoint inside rock' embeds keep occurring at the same rate even WITH the per-step check wired in and forcing a replan on failure -- meaning the embed isn't caused by a stale cached waypoint at all, and the real cause is elsewhere (e.g., a z-frame/waypoint-authoring bug in the same family as the prior 'one z for a whole town' finding, or an index-corruption bug independent of terrain); or (b) the per-step check almost never fires (near-zero triggers) while embeds continue -- meaning colonists are getting INTO the rock some way other than stepping into a waypoint cell that turned solid (e.g., glide/interpolation cutting a corner through a newly-placed block between two still-valid waypoints, which this mechanism would not catch and would need a swept/segment check instead of a single-cell check).

research.question: Any-angle pathing on voxel terrain: is Bastion's fixed SEGMENT_SAMPLES=8 straight-line traversability test the standard mechanism, or is there a cheaper exact test?

mechanisms.game: Theta* (Nash, Koenig & Tovey 2007/2010, 'Theta*: Any-Angle Path Planning on Grids', arxiv.org/abs/1401.3843)
mechanisms.mechanism: LineOfSight(s, s') is a grid-supercover raster test, not fixed-count sampling: a Bresenham/DDA-style line walk enumerates every cell the straight segment actually passes through between s and s', and the test is 'unobstructed' iff none of those cells is blocked. The number of cells checked equals the number of grid cells the segment crosses (grows with |dx|+|dy|, i.e. with segment length/slope), not a constant.
mechanisms.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.3843 (paper); corroborating summary via search of the same paper and https://www.academia.edu/104721348/Theta_for_Any_Angle_Pathfinding — I could not get clean extracted pseudocode text from the PDF fetch (binary/FlateDecode), so the specific 'Bresenham-supercover, count = cells crossed' description is standard-knowledge-plus-secondary-summary rather than a verified direct quote; treat the general mechanism as well-established, the exact pseudocode wording as unverified.
mechanisms.applicability: Directly on point for the core question: the canonical any-angle LOS test is adaptive (proportional to distance/cells crossed), not a fixed sample count. Bastion's fixed N=8 is a deviation from this pattern — it over-samples short 1-2 cell segments and can under-sample (miss cells on) long ones, which matches the exact bug class described ('bump mid-segment...one block apart over six').

mechanisms.game: Lazy Theta* (Nash, Koenig & Tovey, AAAI 2010, 'Lazy Theta*: Any-Angle Path Planning and Path Length Analysis in 3D')
mechanisms.mechanism: Same grid-exact LineOfSight test as Theta*, but the optimization is about WHEN you call it, not HOW: it defers (makes 'lazy') the line-of-sight check to only once per expanded vertex instead of once per visible unexpanded neighbor, cutting LOS-check count by roughly an order of magnitude on 26-neighbor 3D grids without lengthening paths. The per-call test itself is still the exact cell-walk, unchanged.
mechanisms.source: http://idm-lab.org/bib/abstracts/papers/aaai10b.pdf (fetch returned binary-only, saved locally but not text-extractable); corroborated via WebSearch summary of https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/7566 and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/2898607.2898631
mechanisms.applicability: Relevant to Bastion's likely NEXT bottleneck, not the current one: if the 8-sample (or an adaptive cell-walk) LOS test becomes a hot path once called per-neighbor-per-expansion rather than once per committed route, Lazy Theta*'s trick (call it lazily, only when a node is actually expanded, and only against its stored parent) is the standard fix — orthogonal to fixing the sampling exactness itself.

mechanisms.game: Amanatides & Woo, 'A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing' (1987) / Red Blob Games 'supercover' line drawing (redblobgames.com/grids/line-drawing/)
mechanisms.mechanism: The 3D/general form of the same idea: walk the ray through a voxel grid using incremental DDA (integer step + fractional remainder per axis), visiting every voxel/cell the ray enters, in order, with O(1) work per cell and total work proportional to cells traversed. Red Blob Games states this explicitly for the 2D case: cell count = nx+ny (the two axis deltas), an exact, adaptive count, contrasted with plain Bresenham which can skip diagonal-adjacent cells a line clips through.
mechanisms.source: https://www.redblobgames.com/grids/line-drawing/ (fetched, confirmed: 'supercover... guarantees visiting every grid cell a line passes through... adaptive, exact count... cell count = nx+ny'); Amanatides-Woo original paper referenced from that page, not independently fetched.
mechanisms.applicability: This is the most directly transplantable mechanism for Bastion: replace the fixed 8-sample loop over t in [0,1] with an integer DDA/supercover walk over the COLUMNS the segment crosses (Bastion's grid is 2D columns with per-column ground height, so this is literally the 2D supercover case, no z-axis voxel walk needed). Cost becomes proportional to columns actually crossed; correctness becomes exact (every column touched is checked) instead of probabilistic-by-fixed-N.

mechanisms.game: Recast/Detour navmesh toolset (industry-standard, used by Unity/Unreal/Godot integrations)
mechanisms.mechanism: Step-height and slope-walkability are NOT tested at query time at all. Recast bakes them into the mesh during voxelization: input geometry is rasterized into voxels, a triangle/voxel is filtered out as unwalkable if its slope exceeds max-slope or if the vertical gap to the next surface exceeds max-step-height, and only surfaces surviving that filter become navmesh polygons. Detour's runtime raycast/LOS query then only needs to test 2D polygon-edge crossings on the resulting mesh — verticality and step-climbability are already resolved into which polygons exist and connect, so the runtime test is a cheap planar sweep, not a per-query height re-sample.
mechanisms.source: https://recastnav.com/md_Docs_2__1__Introduction.html ; corroborated by WebSearch summaries of https://github.com/recastnavigation/recastnavigation and http://digestingduck.blogspot.com/2009/08/recast-settings-uncovered.html (Recast dev blog on step-height/slope voxelization params) — general architecture description, not a direct pseudocode quote.
mechanisms.applicability: An alternative axis of attack rather than a substitute for the DDA fix: if Bastion's LOS/step-height check is being re-evaluated repeatedly at movement time (per route materialization, per replan) rather than once when a route segment is committed, the Recast pattern says push the step-height filtering into route/graph construction (bake it once into which tile-pairs are declared LOS-clear) so the mover's runtime interpolation never re-tests height at all. Given Bastion's router is already described as 2D with per-column height materialized at waypoint-commit time, this may already be close to how it works — worth confirming where in the pipeline SEGMENT_SAMPLES=8 actually runs (route-build time vs. every tick) before deciding this applies.

mechanisms.game: Baritone (Minecraft pathfinding mod, cabaletta/baritone) and Dwarf Fortress fortress-mode pathing
mechanisms.mechanism: Neither does any-angle/LOS shortcutting at all. Both are pure tile-to-tile A* over a fixed adjacency graph (26-directional in DF's case), where each edge is a named discrete movement primitive (walk, sprint-jump, pillar-up, parkour gap, stairs/ramp) validated by checking the specific blocks/tiles that primitive requires — never a continuous straight-line sample across multiple tiles.
mechanisms.source: https://github.com/cabaletta/baritone (README/USAGE.md, via WebSearch summary); https://dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/v0.34:Path and https://dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/DF2014:Path (via WebSearch summary) — neither fetched directly for full text, general-architecture claims only.
mechanisms.applicability: Negative prior art, useful as a sanity check: the other major voxel-tile colony/agent sims in this space (DF, Minecraft bots) SIDESTEP the exact problem Bastion has by never doing continuous any-angle glide between waypoints more than one tile apart — they just add more graph edges (movement primitives) instead. This confirms Bastion's 'commit to a route, then glide by interpolation between waypoints, verified by LOS' design is closer to Theta*-family robotics/AI pathfinding than to voxel-game convention, so Theta*/Lazy Theta*'s LOS-test literature (not Minecraft/DF) is the right prior art to borrow the sampling mechanism from, not a reason to abandon any-angle interpolation.

research.recommendation: Sampling N points along the segment is NOT the standard approach — it's a known-weaker substitute for the actual standard mechanism, which is an exact, adaptive cell-walk (Bresenham/DDA 'supercover', the same algorithm underlying Theta*'s and Lazy Theta*'s LineOfSight test, and the 2D case of Amanatides-Woo voxel traversal). The standard test enumerates every grid column the straight segment geometrically crosses — cost = number of columns crossed, not a fixed constant — and checks ground height (and step-height delta) at each one. This is strictly better than fixed N=8 in both directions: for a short 2-column hop it does ~2 checks instead of 8 (cheaper), and for a long multi-column segment it checks ALL columns instead of 8 evenly-spaced t-fractions, which is exactly the aliasing failure Bastion already found ('a bump mid-segment... one block apart over six' — a fixed-N sampler run over a segment spanning more columns than N will step over some columns entirely). Recommend replacing SEGMENT_SAMPLES=8 with a 2D integer DDA/supercover walk over the tile columns between the two waypoints (this is cheap: it's the 2D case, no z-axis voxel traversal needed since Bastion already has one ground-height-per-column), checking at each crossed column that (a) the interpolated line height stays within tolerance of that column's ground height and (b) the step-height delta from the previous crossed column is within the movement's climb limit. Separately and orthogonally, if this LOS check is invoked repeatedly at movement/tick time rather than once when a route segment is committed, consider the Recast/Detour pattern of baking step-height-walkability into the route graph once (at commit time) so the mover's interpolation never re-tests height — but that is a placement/architecture decision, not a change to the test's correctness, and is secondary to fixing the sampling exactness itself.
research.what_would_falsify: Pull the actual distribution of committed-route segment lengths (in tile-columns crossed) from a live or logged Bastion town: if essentially all real segments span ≤8 columns (so fixed N=8 never has a gap to miss a column in) AND the LOS check runs rarely enough (once per route-commit, not per-tick) that the extra cost of over-sampling short segments is negligible, then the adaptive DDA walk buys no measurable correctness or performance improvement over the current fixed-8 sampling, and the recommendation would be falsified as unnecessary complexity for this town's actual geometry. Conversely, if any real segment spans >8 columns, or if profiling shows the LOS/segment check is a non-trivial fraction of per-tick or per-route-build cost, that is direct confirmation the adaptive walk is needed exactly as the mechanism predicts (a fixed-N sampler under-samples a >N-column segment by construction, which is a hard geometric fact, not a probabilistic risk).

research.question: What mechanism prevents N colonists from repeatedly failing on the same unreachable/contended item, and which one should feed bastion's claim census (which already counts unreachable_job)?

mechanisms.mechanism: Reachability is precomputed, not discovered by walking. The map is flood-filled into contiguous walkable 'regions' (~12x12 tiles) that share a zone index; the index is recomputed only when the region graph changes structurally (door opens/closes, wall built/removed) — not per query. `Reachability.CanReach` then answers 'can pawn reach target' by comparing region membership/links (cheap, O(regions)) instead of running a full A* that would otherwise scan the whole map before concluding no path exists (this was literally the perf bug the 2013 'Reachability at last' devlog fixes). Crucially, this reachability test is folded into the SAME breadth-first region traversal that WorkGiver_Scanner.ClosestThingReachable already uses to enumerate job candidates, with a validator predicate that ALSO checks 'not forbidden' and 'not already claimed' in that one pass (claim exclusivity is a separate ReservationManager — a flat list of active {target, pawn, stack-count} reservations checked via CanReserve before a job is handed out). Net effect: an unreachable OR already-claimed item is simply invisible to a pawn's candidate search that tick — no pawn ever starts walking toward it, so there is nothing to fail or time out on.
mechanisms.source: https://ludeon.com/blog/2013/07/reachability-at-last/ (devlog, fetch blocked by ludeon.com but corroborated via search snippet: 'optimized flood-fill algorithm... fill out each walkable region with the same zone index... colonist has to check that the region index where they're standing matches the one where they want to go'); region size and hierarchical region-to-region pathfinding corroborated via search of rimworldwiki.com and rimworldhub.com articles; ClosestThingReachable/PotentialWorkThingsGlobal behavior and its 'not forbidden, has job on it' validator corroborated via github.com/josh-m/RW-Decompile (RimWorld/JobGiver_Work.cs) search snippet; ReservationManager reservation-list mechanics read directly from https://github.com/josh-m/RW-Decompile/blob/master/Verse.AI/ReservationManager.cs
mechanisms.applicability: Directly maps onto bastion. Bastion's claim census (bastion-server/src/bastion_jobs.rs) already runs a candidate-time check that distinguishes already_claimed from unreachable_job (census.unreachable_job += 1 at two sites, asserted to sum with already_claimed into not_candidate) — this is structurally the RimWorld 'filter candidates in one pass' idea, already half-built. What bastion is missing is RimWorld's other half: FETCH STALLED and FETCH BUDGET EXPIRED (lines ~27717, ~27748) show colonists still committing a reservation and walking for up to 90s before the runtime discovers the failure the census could have flagged at claim time. The fix is to make the claim-time reachability probe authoritative — refuse the reservation, not just count it — using a cached graph/flood-fill structure over bastion's nav graph (walkable cells/plots), invalidated only on structural change (door, wall, plot edit), not recomputed per fetch.

mechanisms.mechanism: No precheck. Stockpile-driven haul jobs are generated purely from designation state (valid stockpile link + permission), with no test of whether a walkable path actually exists between hauler and item. The dwarf is assigned, walks, and only then discovers no path, producing 'Dwarf cancels task: Could not find path' (general) or 'Dwarf cancels Store Item: Item inaccessible' (hauling-specific — path was open when the job generated but got blocked, e.g. a locked door, or a log repeatedly relocated by river flow). There is no cooldown, blacklist, or cache suppressing re-attempts: per the DF Wiki, 'Stockpiles don't stop generating fetch jobs for items no one is permitted to go to' — the same job is regenerated and handed to the next idle dwarf, which is the documented root of DF's long-running 'cancellation spam' problem (still an open, unmitigated-by-the-engine issue discussed on the current Steam release forums). Community workarounds are entirely manual (forbid the item, break the stockpile link, add material-availability preconditions to work orders) — there is no automatic engine mechanism.
mechanisms.source: https://dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/Dwarf_cancels_task:_Could_not_find_path ; https://dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/Dwarf_cancels_Store_Item:_Item_inaccessible ('Stockpiles don't stop generating fetch jobs for items no one is permitted to go to'; river-flow log example); cancellation-spam-is-unsolved corroborated via https://steamcommunity.com/app/975370/discussions/0/4338725580146492239/ and https://steamcommunity.com/app/975370/discussions/0/597404744772819078/ ('will cancel again and again' if the cause doesn't change)
mechanisms.applicability: This is the anti-pattern bastion is currently exhibiting at the runtime layer (claim -> walk -> fail after up to 90s, repeatable by the next colonist), and DF is direct prior-art evidence that this pattern does NOT self-heal at scale — it is a known, still-open failure class in DF nearly two decades on, mitigated only by manual player intervention, never by an automatic engine fix. This is the pattern to move away from, not toward.

mechanisms.mechanism: Errand ('Chore') eligibility runs through a 'Chore Precondition' system that includes pathability, checked against a maintained nav/reachability grid that is updated on world-change events (build/dig/door toggling) rather than recomputed fresh per errand check — precondition evaluation was reworked to run multithreaded for performance, implying it executes before a duplicant commits to the errand, not after a failed walk. However, this cached grid is a known-imperfect APPROXIMATION: Klei's own bug tracker documents a recurring defect class ('Reachable unreachable build', 'Unreachable task — until a duplicant gets close to it') where a genuinely reachable target (e.g. across water, or behind a half-built ladder) is shown greyed-out/unreachable until a duplicant physically wanders near it, at which point the local grid re-evaluates and the target flips to reachable. So the grid is locally stale far from any duplicant and self-corrects on proximity — the opposite failure mode from DF's true-only-after-walking failures.
mechanisms.source: https://forums.kleientertainment.com/klei-bug-tracker/oni/reachable-unreachable-build-r20562/ (title/topic, full body 403-blocked to fetch tool); corroborating community reports: https://steamcommunity.com/app/457140/discussions/3/1694917906657208205/ ('Unreachable task - until a duplicant gets close to it'); Chore Precondition multithreading rework found via search of oxygennotincluded.wiki.gg patch-notes pages (Versions/U53-642443)
mechanisms.applicability: Partial positive prior art for bastion: precheck-against-a-maintained-cache (not per-request recompute) is the right shape, but ONI shows the failure mode you get if the cache is only kept fresh near active agents — false negatives (flagged unreachable when actually fine) that only clear once someone happens to walk close. Bastion's fix needs a cache that's kept correct colony-wide on structural change, not a proximity-refreshed one, or the 597-at-one-cell tail could be exactly this kind of stale-cache false negative rather than a true unreachability.

research.recommendation: Adopt RimWorld's shape: fold a cheap, CACHED reachability precheck (flood-fill / region-graph over bastion's walkable-cell graph, invalidated only on structural change — door/wall/plot edit, not recomputed per fetch) into the SAME candidate-selection pass that already produces `already_claimed` vs `unreachable_job` in bastion's claim census, and make it authoritative: refuse the reservation at claim time instead of letting the colonist commit and discover the failure 90s later via FETCH STALLED / FETCH BUDGET EXPIRED. Concretely: bastion_jobs.rs already has the RimWorld-shaped half (candidate filtering that distinguishes claimed-vs-unreachable); it's missing the enforcement half (a walk should never start for something the census would have flagged). Do NOT adopt Dwarf Fortress's walk-then-cancel model — it is prior art for what NOT to do; DF's own forums show it never self-heals and is still an open 'cancellation spam' complaint after ~20 years. Take a caution from ONI: whatever cache backs the precheck must be kept correct colony-wide on every structural change, not lazily refreshed only near a colonist, or you trade DF's true-positive-but-late failures for ONI's stale false-negative bug class.
research.what_would_falsify: Pull a sample of the 597 single-cell failures and the 84%-at-ten-cells failures and check, at failure time, whether the target was (a) claimed-but-idle by another colonist (contention, not unreachability — the fix is a RimWorld-style reservation/claim lock, not a reachability precheck) vs (b) genuinely graph-disconnected from the failing colonist (true unreachability — the fix is the region/flood-fill precheck recommended above). If the recommended precheck is implemented and the same population of failures still occurs — i.e., items the cached reachability graph calls 'reachable' still produce FETCH STALLED/BUDGET EXPIRED — that falsifies the precheck as sufficient and points either to a stale-cache bug (ONI's failure mode: the graph wasn't invalidated on the structural change that actually blocked the path) or to a doorway/region-boundary edge case the flood-fill mismodels at exactly the one-cell granularity where 597 of the failures cluster.

research.question: Should hunger be able to kill a Bastion colonist, and if so, through what consequence ladder between 'hungry' and 'dead'?

mechanisms.mechanism: Food need ('saturation') is a 0-100% bar that drains continuously and produces mood thoughts on the way down: below 30% saturation fires 'Hungry' (-6 mood), below 20% fires a larger 'Urgently Hungry' penalty. At 0% saturation a SEPARATE stat appears -- the Malnutrition hediff -- which then climbs on its own at roughly 1.51-2.27% severity per hour REGARDLESS of whether saturation is still 0, through staged symptoms (faster hunger drain, consciousness/manipulation penalties, higher chance of social fights, later loss of consciousness) until it crosses a fixed lethal severity threshold, killing the pawn about 4.9-7.4 days after onset. Feeding the pawn any time before that threshold reverses severity at the same hourly rate with no lasting damage.
mechanisms.applicability: Bastion already has RimWorld's FIRST stat: hunger:NeedTuning (common/src/bastion.rs, decay_per_sec=0.000889) feeds mood_formula's shortfall term, and mood below break_minor (0.25) already arms the Despond breakdown roll -- that IS Bastion's version of the 'Hungry' thought tier. What's missing is RimWorld's SECOND, decoupled stat: a severity value that only starts accumulating once hunger sits at its floor, independent of hunger's own fast-moving value, with its own recoverable-until-lethal staircase.

mechanisms.mechanism: Hunger is a raw counter incrementing ~1/tick (~1200 ticks/day). At 75,000 the dwarf flashes 'Starving' and starts opportunistically eating vermin; at 85,000 it logs a bad thought about starving, feeding the colony's shared happy/unhappy thought pool; at 100,000 it dies outright unless it has stored body fat to burn through first. Thirst runs the same shape on its own clock. Individually these are just one more bad thought, but if enough accumulate fortress-wide relative to good ones, dwarves start throwing tantrums that can chain into a 'tantrum spiral' -- a cascading, colony-wide failure state that a single starvation death can trigger without being the sole cause.
mechanisms.applicability: This is the model closest to a hard, un-forgiving timer: hunger only rises until fed, crossing one fixed numeric line into death, no floor to camp at safely. Bastion's Despond staircase (mood<break_minor arms a sustained-below window then a per-cadence break_chance roll -- forgiving, not an instant flip) is already architecturally DF's tantrum spiral in miniature. A DF-flavored death rule would put a THIRD threshold directly on the hunger value itself (not routed through mood) with its own independent, similarly-forgiving roll.

mechanisms.mechanism: No individual per-colonist need bar at all -- food is a TOWN-LEVEL stock consumed at a fixed per-capita rate (~100 food/person/year). When town production falls behind consumption and the stock runs out, affected houses/citizens show a fork-and-knife 'starving' icon and citizens in that state begin dying directly and in bulk; player reports describe 'dozens' dying within one or two seasons of a shortage taking hold. There is no intermediate malnutrition stage -- the aggregate food balance IS the timer, and death is the fast, direct consequence of that balance staying negative.
mechanisms.applicability: Banished's mechanism is aggregate (town stock), while Bastion's hunger is already per-colonist -- a literal port means discarding NeedTuning/EatFrom for a stock model, a much bigger rewrite than a bolt-on. The Banished-FLAVORED option that actually fits Bastion's architecture is bluntness, not aggregation: keep hunger per-colonist, but once it sits at 0 past a short grace window, roll a flat per-tick death chance with no intermediate stage -- same stakes, same 'colony can crater fast' character, without touching the resource-flow model.

mechanisms.mechanism: Individual death is mechanically SEPARATE from Frostpunk's two societal meters. A citizen who works/lives below 'Comfortable' temperature (or suffers a workplace accident) becomes Sick; an untreated Sick citizen becomes Gravely Ill; an untreated Gravely Ill citizen dies -- a two-stage, treatable-until-the-second-stage ladder gated by a healthcare building as the intervention point. Hope and Discontent are city-wide, not individual: Hope falls as conditions worsen and is deliberately hard to rebuild without spending resources on propaganda/faith buildings; Discontent rising unchecked produces a POLITICAL failure state (the leader is exiled or executed), not more citizen deaths directly. The developers prototyped, then explicitly cut, a mechanic giving amputees a 50% chance of dying by suicide specifically to pressure these meters -- judged too heavy-handed.
mechanisms.applicability: The transferable lesson is architectural: Frostpunk deliberately keeps 'a body fails' (Sick->Gravely Ill->dead, gated by treatment) separate from 'the settlement's will fails' (Hope/Discontent, a policy-level meter with its own failure state). Bastion already has that split by accident -- hunger/mood/Despond is the individual layer, and there is no settlement-level meter yet. If hunger death ships, this argues for keeping it a personal, treatable ladder parallel to Despond rather than routing it through the shared mood pool, so a colonist fed in time recovers exactly like a treated Sick pawn.

mechanisms.mechanism: Hunger is one of several bars. Left empty, status escalates through named moodlets -- 'Hungry' -> 'Very Hungry'/'Starving' (Sims 3) or 'Ravenous' (Sims 4) -- during which the Sim is described as practically non-functioning. If that terminal moodlet's OWN timer expires before eating, the Sim dies of starvation over roughly a couple of real days of neglect; eating at any point before that fully cancels the countdown with no lingering effect. The game explicitly exempts specific populations: babies/toddlers/children are removed by a social-worker NPC before they can starve, and pregnant Sims cannot starve at all.
mechanisms.applicability: Closest existing shape to Bastion's own mood/Despond system: a need empties, produces an escalating STATUS that visibly incapacitates before anything permanent happens, and only the final stage's own timer running out is lethal -- exactly Despond's preempt-everything shape. Sims' protected-population carve-out raises a question Bastion hasn't faced yet: if hunger can kill, does it kill every colonist uniformly, or are some states/roles exempt the way Sims exempts the young and pregnant?

mechanisms.mechanism: No hunger meter and no starvation death in the base game. Food is a buff-item only: eating restores/buffs energy (stamina) and grants temporary stat bonuses; NOT eating carries zero direct penalty -- stamina hitting 0 just blocks stamina-costing actions until restored by sleep or food. Several community mods (Simple Hunger System, Another Hunger Mod, Survivalistic) exist specifically to bolt a hunger-to-starvation-damage pipeline onto a base game that deliberately omits one.
mechanisms.applicability: This is close to Bastion's CURRENT behavior (hunger decays, EatFrom is an opportunity not an obligation, zero does nothing) minus the buff angle. Stardew shows 'no consequence' is a legitimate shipped design for a calm-production game -- but the fact its own community immediately modded starvation back in is the counter-signal: players who want colony-sim stakes treat a hunger bar with no floor consequence as a missing feature, not a design statement.

mechanisms.mechanism: No needs system of any kind exists for player or villagers -- no hunger, thirst, or stamina meter. Design commentary frames this as deliberate: the game trades survival pressure for a slower, real-time-clock-driven loop of cultivating and decorating, built to be stress-free rather than to withhold consequences for a tracked need.
mechanisms.applicability: Not directly applicable -- Bastion already tracks hunger with a decay rate, a mood penalty, and a dedicated EatFrom job; the pressure has already been introduced. Animal Crossing's stance is 'never introduce the need,' not 'introduce it and then do nothing at the floor,' so it offers no template for Bastion's actual situation.

research.recommendation:
No single mechanism to crown -- this is explicitly the judgement call the charter reserves for Ben, so what follows is three coherent, ready-to-build options rather than a pick.

OPTION A -- RimWorld-style graduated ladder (recommended DEFAULT if Ben wants one). Add a second stat, `malnutrition` severity, that only accumulates while hunger sits pinned at 0 (decoupled from hunger's own fast value, mirroring RimWorld's saturation/malnutrition split). Crossing tuned thresholds stages in: a work-speed penalty layered on the existing mood shortfall, then a forced-incapacitated 'Collapsed' job state (a new preempting arm alongside Despond/RestAt/EatFrom), then at a final threshold, death -- fully recoverable by eating at every stage but the last, timed in game-days so it actually surfaces before 16 days pass unremarked. Cost: highest -- new per-colonist field, thresholds tuned against mood_formula so the two systems don't double-penalize, and Bastion has NO death/corpse/population-decrement/replacement plumbing today, so 'colonist dies' needs that built regardless of which option ships. Payoff: fits the existing shortfall->Despond architecture almost exactly and gives the clearest, most-warned, most reversible-until-the-end ladder -- the pattern the project's own Despond system already chose (sustained-below window, forgiving per-cadence roll, not an instant flip).

OPTION B -- Banished-style blunt death roll. No new stat: once hunger has sat at its floor past a short grace window (a timer on the existing value), start rolling a flat per-colonist death chance every tick/cadence until fed. No intermediate incapacitation stage. Cost: cheapest to build (a timer + a roll) but the highest-risk option given Bastion's own measured history -- population growth is already fragile (colony metrics vary 2-3x run to run per standing note, and a one-shot resource nothing re-adds can only shrink), so an unconditional roll compounds badly with any transient hunger stall that is really EatFrom job-pipeline latency rather than genuine famine, with no warning stage to catch the difference first. Still needs the death/population plumbing Option A needs, on a shorter fuse.

OPTION C -- Escalating incapacitation, no death (Sims/Frostpunk-flavored floor without the drop). Reuse the Despond machinery directly: hunger sitting at 0 past a grace window forces a 'Starving' preempting self-job (same shape as Despond, harder to shake, blocks all other claims) that is loud and costly but never kills; eating clears it immediately. Cost: smallest possible lift -- no new stat, no death/corpse/population plumbing at all, just one more arm on the pattern JobKind already uses for Despond/RestAt/EatFrom, gated on sustained hunger==0 instead of mood. Directly answers the observed symptom (16 days at fed=0 with nothing distinguishable happening) by making that state visible and expensive. Tradeoff: never delivers the permanent-loss stakes RimWorld/DF/Banished are actually known for, so it's a half-measure if the goal is survival-game tension rather than just making zero-hunger legible.

If forced to default: Option A costs the most up front but is the only one that reuses Bastion's existing shortfall/mood/Despond machinery on BOTH ends (a real 'hungry' penalty already exists, so it only needs a second stat for the 'starving' extension) rather than building a parallel system (B) or stopping short of the stakes decision entirely (C).
research.what_would_falsify: Before trusting ANY sustained-zero death/incapacitation gate (Options A or B), measure how much of a colonist's time at hunger==0 in a NORMALLY-SUPPLIED colony is real scarcity versus EatFrom job-pipeline latency (claim/haul/travel delay on the pre-claimed EatFrom job, per the B7-3 NEED-CHECK pass). If colonists routinely sit at hunger=0 for meaningful stretches purely as a queuing artifact -- not because food is actually short -- then any threshold timed off raw hunger will fire background attrition or forced-collapse on well-fed colonies, which falsifies the gate as designed and means the sustained-zero window must be calibrated against measured EatFrom latency, not assumed, before a death or Collapsed threshold is set. Separately, for Option A specifically: if death is added but no downstream consumer exists (no corpse/removal, no population-count effect visible to the player, no ripple into other colonists' mood), the mechanism is dead code wearing a threshold -- exactly the class of gap the project's own 'a consumer turns a saturated par into live demand' finding warns about.

research.question: Activity tallies (time-held vs event counts): how do RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, Oxygen Not Included, and agent-based sims compute 'what does this agent spend its time on', and how do they separate needs from work in the denominator? Is bastion's per-sweep-while-holding-a-non-personal-job tally (excluding rest/recreation) the standard shape? What should the colonist inspector show?

mechanisms.mechanism: No built-in OBSERVED time-use tally exists. Two separate systems instead: (a) Need meters (Rest, Food, Joy, etc.) decay continuously and only force a behavior switch away from work at fixed thresholds — rest<30%, food<30%, joy<35% — while an 'Anything' schedule block defaults to work; (b) the Schedule tab is a 24-column x pawn grid the player PAINTS by hand with Sleep/Work/Joy/Recreation/Anything brushes. That grid is intention, not a record of what actually happened that day.
mechanisms.source: https://rimworldwiki.com/wiki/Needs ; https://rimworldaccess.com/colony/schedule/ ; corroborated by third-party mods that exist only to fill this gap — Steam Workshop 'Pawn Tracker' (id 3072118260) and 'Better Records Tab' (id 2359778562)
mechanisms.applicability: RimWorld offers no genre baseline for bastion's tally question: its closest analog (the Schedule tab) is a PLANNED allocation, structurally different from an observed/measured one. The community demand for tracker mods is itself evidence that vanilla shipped colony sims commonly lack this feature, not that they solved it well.

mechanisms.mechanism: The labor system explicitly enumerates jobs 'not associated with a labor': eating, drinking, sleeping, going on break, partying, cleaning themselves, resting. These are automatic and excluded from the labor/skill taxonomy BY DEFINITION, not by measurement. Separately, the Unit list / task menu shows each dwarf's CURRENT job as a live point-in-time label (sortable, refreshed continuously) — not a duration-weighted history. No built-in tally of time-spent-per-category exists anywhere in the game.
mechanisms.applicability: Directly validates bastion's choice to EXCLUDE rest/recreation from the tally — DF's own labor taxonomy draws exactly that line categorically. But DF sets no precedent for HOW to measure: its own UI is pure point-sampling (current job as a label), which is the weaker of the two failure modes this session already moved past.

mechanisms.mechanism: The Schedule screen is again a PLANNED grid (Work / Downtime / Bedtime blocks, player-painted), not measured. Inside a block, priority rules decide behavior — e.g. during Downtime a duplicant checks bathroom (bladder>40%) then hunger (<3300 kcal) then leisure, falling back to work only if none apply. The Errand system ranks ~15 work categories by priority, and a duplicant finishes its CURRENT errand before re-evaluating a higher-priority one — no mid-task preemption.
mechanisms.applicability: Same shape as RimWorld's schedule grid: planned, not observed — genre-wide pattern, not a bastion-specific gap. ONI's non-preemption rule (finish the current errand first) parallels bastion holding a job across a sweep, which is a reasonable structural analog even though ONI never turns it into a time tally.

mechanisms.game: Real-world standard: US Bureau of Labor Statistics American Time Use Survey (ATUS)
mechanisms.mechanism: The actual professional method for 'what does an agent spend its time on': a 24-hour diary recall (4am-to-4am) where respondents report DURATION in minutes per activity, summing to 1440 minutes/day — duration-weighted by construction, never an event count. Results are conventionally published as proportional/pie breakdowns into major categories, with Personal Care (sleep, hygiene, eating — i.e. NEEDS) held as a category distinct from Work and Work-Related Activities and from Leisure and Sports (i.e. RECREATION).
mechanisms.applicability: This is the real prior art for the session's fix: duration-weighted (time-held), never event-count, with needs categorically separated from work — exactly what the tally correction did. It is also the standard justification for a per-agent PIE as the presentation: ATUS itself is conventionally shown to the public as a pie of 'how the average day breaks down.'

mechanisms.game: Agent-based simulation on Time Use Survey data (SMACH / residential load-curve ABMs)
mechanisms.mechanism: Agents' daily task sequences are generated from TUS duration data (quantitative) combined with qualitative activity-selection heuristics. Full internal accounting mechanism (exact needs/work split in the model's own bookkeeping) was not retrievable — only the abstract was accessible, not the full paper.
mechanisms.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07966 — abstract only; treat as partially verified, from memory beyond that unverified
mechanisms.applicability: Weak corroboration that duration-weighted diary data, not event counts, is the standard INPUT for agent daily-activity modeling in the wider ABM literature — consistent with the ATUS finding but not independently confirmed at the mechanism level.

research.recommendation: Keep bastion's current tally shape (accumulate per sweep while holding a non-personal job; exclude rest/recreation from the numerator) — it already matches the one real methodological standard found (ATUS: duration-weighted, needs held in a separate category by construction) and DF's own design principle that needs are categorically not labor. Do not revert toward event/arrival counts. For the colonist inspector, present it as a per-colonist PIE with slices Work / Needs (sleep+eat, mirroring DF's exclusion list and ATUS's 'Personal Care') / Recreation / Idle-unassigned, computed directly from the existing sweep-accumulation (slice weight = sweeps-in-category / total-sweeps-alive) — no new instrument needed, only a new denominator and per-bucket accumulator. This is the one genre-adjacent precedent found (ATUS's own public 'how the day breaks down' pie); no shipped colony sim (RimWorld, DF, ONI) has an observed per-agent time-use view to imitate instead — their closest features (Schedule tab / Cycles schedule) show PLANNED intent, which bastion has no player-authored equivalent for, so a colored 24-hour schedule strip should be at most a secondary/optional view later, not the primary one now.
research.what_would_falsify: If, once wired into the inspector, the pie reads nearly identical across most colonists regardless of role (e.g. everyone shows ~85% work regardless of job), the sweep-holding tally lacks per-colonist resolution and just restates the population-level stat already reported elsewhere — falsifying the pie as a useful diagnostic. Also falsified if typical job durations turn out to be shorter than or comparable to the sweep period itself: then sweep-count under-resolves short jobs the same way raw arrival-count over-counted them in the original bug, and the tally (not just its presentation) needs a sub-sweep timestamp before any inspector view built on it can be trusted.
